q: 1. The unit of measurement of long thin work like skirting, handrail, cornice, coping, bedding etc. is
explain: Linear works where the cross-section is uniform and length is the primary measurement are recorded in running metres (per m).

q: 2. A document containing detailed description of all items of work (but their quantities are not mentioned) together with their current rates is called
explain: The Schedule of Rates (SOR) is a list containing the description of items and their sanctioned rates, used as a reference for preparing estimates.

q: 3. The essential requirements to prepare a good estimate are
options: a full dimensioned drawing to scale
explain: To prepare an accurate estimate, one needs the dimensions (drawings), the quality of work (specifications), and the cost per unit (SOR).

q: 4. The portion which is wrongly excavated by the contractor is to be filled by
options: the earth excavated from the same pit
earth excavated from far away from the site
explain: If a contractor over-excavates a foundation, they must fill the excess depth with concrete (usually 1:4:8 or as specified) at their own cost to ensure structural stability.

q: 5. The quantity of wood of the shutters of doors and windows is calculated in
explain: While the door frames (chowkhats) are measured in m³, the shutters (panes/panels) are measured by surface area in square meters (m²).

q: 6. The nominal lead and lift allowed for the earthwork in the excavations of the foundations are
explain: Standard specifications allow for a normal lead (horizontal distance) of 30m and a normal lift (vertical distance) of 1.5m in general earthwork.

q: 7. No deductions are made in the masonry for the openings if the area of the opening does not exceed
explain: Per IS codes, deductions are not required for small openings (like ventilation or pipe holes) up to 0.1 square meters in area.

q: 8. For electric wiring such as fan, light, plug etc., the estimate is made in terms of
options: total load at main in KW
total length of wiring in metres
explain: Electrical installations in buildings are generally estimated by counting the number of 'points' (each light, fan, or socket outlet is one point).

q: 9. The amount required to be deposited by a contractor while submitting a tender is known as
explain: Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) is a small percentage of the estimate cost (usually 2-3%) paid by bidders to ensure they are serious about the contract.

q: 10. The brick work is measured in sq. metre, in case of
options: half brick walls or the partition
explain: All the mentioned types (honeycomb, soling, and half-brick partitions) are thin or specialized brickworks where area is the standard unit of measurement.

q: 11. The portion which is wrongly excavated by the contractor is to be filled by
options: the earth excavated from the same pit
the earth excavated from a borrow pit far away from the site
explain: If a contractor over-excavates foundation trenches, they must fill the excess depth with concrete of the same specification as the foundation, at their own cost.

q: 12. The plan of a building is in the form of a rectangle with center line dimensions of outer walls as 9.7 m x 14.7 m. The thickness of the wall in super structure is 0.30 m. Then its plinth area is
13. In long and short wall method of estimation, the length of long wall is the centre to centre distance between the walls and
options: one fourth breadth of wall on each side
half breadth of wall on each side
explain: To find the out-to-out length of a long wall, you take the center-to-center distance and add half the width of the wall at each end (Total = C/C + 1 Full Width).

q: 14. The quantity for expansion joint in buildings is worked out in
explain: Expansion joints are typically measured by their length in running meters (m).

q: 15. The rate of an item of work depends on
explain: The unit rate is influenced by the quality of materials, the ratio of the mix (like 1:3 vs 1:6 mortar), and the complexity of the work description.

q: 16. The measurement of still grills is taken in terms of
explain: Steel items like grills, gates, and reinforcement bars are measured by weight (kg or quintal).

q: 17. The volume of cement required for 10 m³ of brickwork in 1:6 cement mortar is approximately equal to
explain: Brickwork requires about 30% mortar. For 10 m³, we need 3 m³ of mortar. Cement = (1/7) * 3 = 3/7 m³.

q: 18. In the estimation of plastering surface the deductions are not made for
explain: For plastering, no deductions are made for very small areas like beam ends or openings under 0.5 m², and no additions are made for jambs/soffits of such openings.

q: 19. In the case of roof truss made of steel, rivets, bolts, and nuts usually account for
explain: An allowance of 5% of the total weight of the steel members is usually added to account for connecting rivets, bolts, and nuts.

q: 20. For electric wiring such as fan, light, plug, the estimate is made in terms of
options: total load at main in kw
total length of wiring in metres.
explain: Internal electrical wiring is generally estimated by counting the 'number of points' (light point, fan point, etc.).

q: 21. End lap provided in asbestos cement sheets is equal to
explain: For normal slopes, an end lap (vertical overlap) of 15 cm is the standard requirement.

q: 22. Whenever the whitewashing or distempering is done on corrugated iron sheets, in the estimation the plan area of that sheets is increased by
explain: Corrugated iron (CI) sheets have a larger actual surface area than their flat plan area; a 14% increase is typically allowed for painting/whitewashing.

q: 23. Whenever colour washing on a.c.. corrugated sheets is done, in the estimation the plane area of the sheets is increased by
explain: Asbestos Cement (AC) corrugated sheets have deeper corrugations than CI sheets, requiring a higher allowance (20%) for surface area.

q: 24. Arrange the specific weights of wood (W), cement (C), steel (S) and coarse aggregate (A) in the decreasing order.
explain: Steel (~7850 kg/m³) > Cement (~1440 kg/m³) > Coarse Aggregate (~1200-1400 kg/m³) > Wood (~600-800 kg/m³). Note: Answer key indicates option B, but scientifically Steel is heaviest.

q: 25. Unit of measurement of supply of brick is
explain: Bricks are manufactured as individual units and are supplied, counted, and paid for by number (usually per 1000 units).

q: 26. The weight of 10 mm diameter mild steel rod per metre length is equal to
explain: The weight is calculated using the formula d²/162. So, (10 * 10) / 162 = 0.617 kg/m, rounded to 0.62 kg.

q: 27. The unit of measurement of terrazzo or marble or tile flooring is
explain: Flooring is a surface treatment and is measured by the total area covered in square metres (m²).

q: 28. Which department looks after the execution and maintenance of water supply and sanitary works?
explain: The Department of Water Supply and Sewerage (or PHED in many regions) specifically handles public health engineering tasks like water and sanitation.

q: 29. The most reliable estimate is
explain: A detailed estimate is prepared based on actual measurements from drawings and is therefore the most accurate and reliable.

q: 30. Due to change in price level, a revised estimate is prepared if the sanctioned estimate exceeds
explain: A revised estimate must be prepared if the actual expenditure or the probable cost exceeds the sanctioned amount by more than 5%.

q: 31. The plinth area of a building includes
options: area of walls at floor level
explain: While internal areas like walls and lifts are part of the built-up area, common estimation rules often distinguish what constitutes 'Plinth' vs 'Carpet'. The key indicates cantilevered porches (if covered) are often included.

q: 32. Carpet area does not include the area of
explain: Carpet area is the actual usable area where a carpet can be laid. It excludes walls, balconies, toilets, kitchens, and corridors.

q: 33. The floor area includes the area of the balcony up to
explain: In many building bylaws, only 50% of the balcony area is counted towards the total floor area or Floor Space Index (FSI).

q: 34. The measurement is made in square metre in case of
explain: Concrete foundation and RCC work are measured in cubic metres (m³), and hollow block walls are also typically measured in m³ (unless very thin).

q: 35. The area of the segmental portion of an arch with span l and riser r is approximately given by
explain: The area of a parabolic or shallow segmental arch is roughly calculated as two-thirds of the product of the span and the rise (2/3 × l × r).

q: 36. The measurement is not made in square metres in case of
explain: RCC Chhajjas (projections) are often measured in cubic metres or as a specific item, whereas DPC and formwork are strictly square metre items.

q: 37. The measurement is made for stone work in square metre in case of
explain: Thin stone veneer or wall facing is measured in m², whereas massive stone structures like columns are in m³; however, combined options often point to area-based cladding.

q: 38. The area is measured correct to the nearest
explain: In estimation, all area measurements are recorded to two decimal places, i.e., 0.01 square metres.

q: 39. The volume is measured correct to the nearest
explain: Volume calculations are standardly recorded to two decimal places (0.01 m³).

q: 40. While preparing a detailed estimate
explain: The standard degree of accuracy for dimensions, areas, and volumes in engineering estimates is 0.01 units.

q: 41. The 'center line method' is specially adopted for estimating
explain: The centerline method is the fastest way to estimate quantities for buildings with uniform cross-sections, especially those with circular or polygonal plans.

q: 42. In long and short wall method... length of long wall is the center to center distance plus
options: half breadth of wall on each side
explain: Long wall length = (C/C distance) + (1/2 breadth + 1/2 breadth) = (C/C distance) + Breadth.

q: 43. While estimating a reinforced cement structure, the omitted cover of concrete is assumed
explain: Standard concrete covers (end, side, and bottom) must be subtracted from member dimensions to find the actual length of reinforcement bars.

q: 44. The damp proof course (DPC) is measured in
explain: DPC is a thin layer applied over the plinth; since its thickness is very small and specified, it is measured by area (m²).

q: 45. The rate of an item of work depends on
explain: The unit rate is influenced by the quality of materials (specs), the mix ratio (proportion), and how the work is performed (method).

q: 46. The detention period in a septic tank is assumed
explain: While the key indicates 30 minutes (c), in practical engineering, the detention period for a septic tank is actually 24 to 48 hours. (Referencing the provided key).

q: 47. The trap which is provide to disconnect the house drain from the street sewer is called
explain: All these terms refer to the Intercepting Trap located at the last point of the house drainage system before it joins the public sewer.

q: 48. Anti-siphonage pipe is connected to
options: Bottom of P trap W. C.
Top of P trap W. C.
explain: Anti-siphonage pipes are connected to the top of the P-trap to prevent the water seal from being sucked out by atmospheric pressure changes.

q: 49. The cross-sections for a highway is taken at
options: right angle to the center line
explain: Highway cross-sections are surveyed perpendicularly to the alignment at regular intervals (usually 30m) and where the terrain changes significantly.

q: 50. If B is the width of formation, d is the height of embankment, side slope S : 1... the area of cross-section is
explain: Area of a trapezoidal embankment section = Area of central rectangle (B*d) + Area of two side triangles (2 * 1/2 * Sd * d) = Bd + Sd².
